cards.q: What is DiffServ and why is it the de-facto enterprise/SP QoS model?
cards.a: DiffServ is the QoS architecture where each packet carries its own class in the DSCP field and each router applies a per-hop behavior (PHB). It has no signaling and no reservations, so it scales well and is the de-facto model for enterprise/SP QoS.

cards.q: How do DiffServ and IntServ differ in model, signaling, scale, and guarantee?
cards.a: DiffServ is per-class with no signaling, excellent scale, and statistical guarantees; IntServ is per-flow with RSVP signaling, poor scale, and hard guarantees.

cards.q: What are the DSCP and ECN fields and what does PHB mean?
cards.a: DSCP is 6 bits (packet class), ECN is 2 bits (congestion marks), and PHB is the treatment applied per class by each router. DSCP selects the PHB each router applies.

cards.q: What PHBs map to voice, video conferencing, video stream, signaling, and control?
cards.a: EF (46) = voice/low latency, AF4x (34/36/38) = video conferencing, AF3x (26/28/30) = video stream, AF2x (18/20/22) = signaling/OAM, and CSx/CS6 = control.

cards.q: How is AF traffic structured and what does the third digit mean?
cards.a: AF classes (AF1x-AF4x) have three drop precedences where x1 is low drop, x2 is medium, and x3 is high. Within an AF class, lower drop number = lower drop probability = better survival.

cards.q: In the DiffServ model, what does the edge versus core do with traffic?
cards.a: The edge classifies and marks once; the core trusts and applies PHBs consistently (e.g., CBWFQ/WRED), and the provider honors the DSCP or contract.

cards.q: How should EF, AF, and best effort be treated in a QoS policy?
cards.a: EF goes to LLQ (priority), AF to bandwidth plus WRED (random-detect dscp-based), and best effort to the default class/bandwidth.

cards.q: A PHB is not being applied to traffic; what is the likely cause and check?
cards.a: There is no service-policy attached to the interface. Check the policy-map and its attachment.

cards.q: All AF traffic in a class is being dropped; what is the likely cause and check?
cards.a: Wrong drop precedence (e.g., x3 high-drop) or a bad random-detect drop profile. Check the DSCP in the class-map and the WRED drop thresholds.

cards.q: What DSCP value and PHB is used for voice, and how many drop levels does AF have?
cards.a: EF (46) is voice; AF (Assured Forwarding) has three drop levels/precedences per class.

cards.q: Does DiffServ use signaling or reservations?
cards.a: No, DiffServ has no signaling and no reservations; it relies on DSCP and PHB, and is statistical rather than hard-guaranteed.

cards.q: What is the difference between DiffServ and IntServ guarantees?
cards.a: DiffServ provides statistical guarantees per class; IntServ provides hard, per-flow guarantees.
